fields.title: The First Letter to the Thessalonians
fields.subtitle: Pros Thessalonikeis A, “First to the Thessalonians”
fields.description: Very likely the oldest of Paul’s letters, written around AD 50 to a church he had been driven away from only months before: Gentiles who had “turned to God from idols” and were already suffering for it. Paul gives thanks for their faith, love and hope, remembers how he lived among them like a nursing mother and a father, and tells of the joy Timothy’s news has brought. Then he urges them on in holiness, love and quiet work, comforts them over believers who have died with the hope of the Lord’s coming, and ends with words learned by heart ever since: be joyful at all times, never stop praying, give thanks whatever happens. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the First Letter to the Thessalonians?
qa.answer: A letter from Paul, with Silvanus (Silas) and Timothy, to the young church in Thessalonica, the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia. Paul had founded the church on his second missionary journey and been forced to leave (Acts 17:1–10). The letter gives thanks for the believers’ faith, defends how Paul lived among them, encourages them under persecution, teaches them how to live in holiness and love, and comforts them about believers who have died.

qa.question: Who wrote 1 Thessalonians, and when?
qa.answer: The apostle Paul, who names himself with Silvanus and Timothy in the first verse. Almost all scholars accept it as his. He wrote from Corinth, soon after Timothy returned from Thessalonica with news of the church (3:6), around AD 50 or 51. That makes it very likely the earliest of Paul’s letters that survive, and perhaps the oldest writing in the New Testament, though some date Galatians earlier.

qa.question: Why did Paul write 1 Thessalonians?
qa.answer: He had left Thessalonica in a hurry, after only a short stay, and feared that persecution had shaken the new believers. When Timothy brought good news, Paul wrote to thank God for them, to answer those who said he was a travelling preacher out for money, to strengthen them in holiness and love, and to answer a question troubling them: what happens to believers who die before the Lord comes?

qa.question: What does 1 Thessalonians 4 teach about the second coming?
qa.answer: That believers who have died are not lost. When the Lord comes down from heaven, “the dead who belong to Christ will rise first”, and the living will be swept up with them to meet the Lord, and “from then on we will be with the Lord always” (4:16–17). Christians differ over how this fits other passages: many evangelicals see here a rapture of believers before a time of tribulation, while others read it as the single return of Christ in glory, with the church going out to welcome him as a city welcomed an arriving king. Paul’s own aim is comfort: “So comfort one another with these words.”

qa.question: What does “never stop praying” mean in 1 Thessalonians 5:17?
qa.answer: It comes in a group of three short commands: “Be joyful at all times. Never stop praying. Whatever happens, give thanks; this is what God wants for you in Christ Jesus” (5:16–18). Paul does not mean that believers should do nothing but pray, since the same letter tells them to work with their hands. He means a life turned toward God at every moment, returning to prayer again and again through the day, as he himself prayed for the Thessalonians “night and day” (3:10).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Everywhere people tell of the welcome you gave us, and how you turned to God from idols, to be servants of the living and true God and to wait for his Son from heaven. God raised him from the dead: Jesus, who rescues us from the wrath that is coming.

— 1 Thessalonians 1:9–10

Some time around AD 50, in the city of Corinth, Paul wrote to a church he had been forced to leave only a few months before. It is very likely the oldest of his letters that we have, and so perhaps the oldest Christian writing of any kind to survive. Before any of the Gospels had been written down, a small congregation in a Greek port city was hearing this letter read aloud.

Here, within twenty years of the cross, is a church that already prays to God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ together and waits for Jesus to come from heaven. And here is a missionary writing not as a theologian at a desk but as a parent separated from his children too soon. He cannot stop thanking God for them, and he cannot stop worrying about them.

A church founded in a hurry

Thessalonica, today Thessaloniki, was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia. Named after a half-sister of Alexander the Great, it stood on the Via Egnatia, the great road that crossed the Balkans from the Adriatic to the Aegean, and it had a busy harbour. News travelled fast from such a place, as Paul says it did (1:8).

Acts 17 tells how the church began. Paul, Silas and Timothy came on from Philippi, where Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed. For three Sabbaths Paul reasoned in the synagogue that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead, and that Jesus was the Messiah. Some Jews believed, together with a large number of God-fearing Greeks and a good many leading women. Then a mob attacked the house of a believer named Jason, the missionaries were accused of proclaiming another king, Jesus, and they were sent away by night.

The stay may have been longer than three weeks (compare 2:9 and Philippians 4:16), but it was short, and it ended in danger. Paul went on to Berea and then to Athens. Unable to bear not knowing how the new believers were standing up to the pressure, he sent Timothy back to them. When Timothy returned with good news, Paul, now in Corinth, wrote this letter. An inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio, the governor before whom Paul was brought in Corinth (Acts 18:12), to about AD 51, so the letter can be dated more securely than almost anything else in the New Testament.

Most of the church were Gentiles. They had “turned to God from idols”, which no Jewish believer would need to do, and their own people had turned against them for it (2:14). They had no New Testament, no buildings and very little teaching. What they had was the word they had welcomed, the Spirit, one another, and this letter.

The shape of the letter

  • Chapters 1–3: thanksgiving and a story. Paul gives thanks for the church’s faith, recalls how the gospel came to them and how he lived among them, and tells how he sent Timothy and what joy his news has brought.
  • Chapters 4–5: how to live while waiting. Holiness in the body, love in the family of believers, quiet work, the hope for those who have died, the day of the Lord, and a string of short commands for the life of the church.

Each half ends with a prayer for the church to be kept holy at the coming of the Lord Jesus (3:11–13; 5:23–24), the horizon of the whole letter.

Faith, love and hope

In its third verse the letter names three things Paul remembers about the Thessalonians: the work their faith does, the labour their love takes on, and the endurance their hope gives them. The same three return near the end, as armour: “faith and love for our breastplate and the hope of salvation for our helmet” (5:8). It is probably the earliest place in Christian writing where faith, love and hope appear together, a few years before Paul wrote of them again in 1 Corinthians 13.

Notice how active they are. Faith does work; love labours; hope endures.

Like a nursing mother

Chapter 2 is Paul’s account of how he lived among them, and it reads like a reply to slander. Travelling speakers in the Greek world were often in it for money and applause, and someone seems to have said Paul was one more of them. He answers by reminding them of what they saw. He never used flattery and never put on a show to cover up greed. He worked night and day so as not to be a burden. And he reaches for the tenderest pictures he can find:

Our longing for you was such that we gladly gave you not only the gospel of God but ourselves too, for you had become dear to us.

— 1 Thessalonians 2:8

He was gentle among them, like a nursing mother with her children; he urged and comforted them, as a father treats his own children; and when he was torn away, he felt orphaned himself.

The same chapter holds one of the hardest passages in Paul’s letters (2:14–16), where he speaks of the Jews of Judea “who killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets and drove us out”. A few scholars have thought it was added later; most accept it as Paul’s, written in the heat of persecution. It needs to be read with care. Paul is comparing the Thessalonians’ sufferings at the hands of their own people with those of the Judean churches, themselves Jewish, at the hands of theirs. He was a Jew himself, and in Romans 9–11 he writes of his own people with anguish and hope. Whatever these lines mean, they cannot mean a verdict on the Jewish people as a whole.

Now we can truly live again

Chapter 3 is the story of an anxious wait. Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy, his “brother and God’s fellow worker in the gospel of Christ”, to strengthen the church. He feared that the tempter had got to them and that all his work had come to nothing. Then Timothy came back:

But Timothy has just come back to us from you, with the good news of your faith and love. He tells us that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you. So, brothers and sisters, in all our distress and trouble your faith has given us comfort about you. Now we can truly live again, if you are standing firm in the Lord.

— 1 Thessalonians 3:6–8

Paul’s own life, he tells them, hung on whether they were standing firm. The chapter ends in prayer, that the Lord would make their love overflow and their hearts stand firm until the day he comes “with all his holy ones”.

This is God’s will for you

The second half begins with instruction, though Paul insists the Thessalonians already know it and are already doing it; they need only do so “more and more”. First comes holiness: “This is God’s will for you: that you be holy.” New believers from a pagan world had to learn to keep away from sexual immorality. Then love for one another, which God himself has taught them. Then, more surprisingly, a quiet life: “Be eager to live calmly, look after your own affairs and earn your living with your hands.”

Paul does not say why. Perhaps some believers, sure that the Lord was coming soon, had stopped working. The theme returns at 5:14 and much more sharply in 2 Thessalonians 3. Hope in the Lord’s coming, Paul thinks, should make a person more faithful in ordinary work, not less.

Those who have fallen asleep

Then Paul turns to a question that had clearly been troubling the church. Since he left, some believers had died. Would they miss the Lord’s coming? Had they lost their share in the hope? Paul answers:

We do not want you to be left in the dark, brothers and sisters, about those who have fallen asleep, so that you do not grieve as others do who have no hope. We believe that Jesus died and rose again; and in the same way, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep.

— 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14

He does not forbid grief, only grieving “as others do who have no hope”. Then he describes the Lord’s coming: a shout of command, an archangel’s call, the sound of God’s trumpet; the dead in Christ rising first, and the living swept up with them “into the clouds to meet the Lord in the air”.

Christians have read these verses in different ways. The Latin Bible’s word for “swept up” gave English the word rapture, and many evangelical Christians, especially since the nineteenth century, have taught that believers will be taken from the earth before a time of great tribulation, with the Lord’s visible return following later. Many others read it as the single return of Christ in glory: the word for “meet” was used when a city’s people went out to welcome an arriving ruler and escort him in. Paul is not answering our questions about timing. He ends with the point that matters most to him and to his grieving readers: “From then on we will be with the Lord always.” And then, “So comfort one another with these words.”

Like a thief at night

About times and dates, Paul says, they know all they need: the day of the Lord comes like a thief at night. It will surprise those who say “All is peaceful and safe”. But believers are “children of light and children of the day”, so the right response is not calculation but readiness: to stay awake, keep a clear head, and put on faith, love and hope. And they need not fear:

For God did not destine us for wrath. He destined us to gain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that, awake or asleep, we may live with him together.

— 1 Thessalonians 5:9–10

“Awake or asleep”: living or dead, believers belong to the one who died for them.

Be joyful at all times

The letter ends with a burst of short commands for the life of a young church. Respect those who lead and work hard among you. Keep peace. Correct the idle, encourage the fainthearted, stand by the weak, be patient with everyone. Never pay back harm with harm. And then three lines that have been learned by heart ever since:

Be joyful at all times. Never stop praying. Whatever happens, give thanks; this is what God wants for you in Christ Jesus.

— 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18

Paul is not commanding a mood but describing a life turned toward God at every moment. “Never stop praying” has been taken up by Christians in every century, from the desert monks who repeated a short prayer through the day to the lay brother in a Paris kitchen who learned to practise the presence of God among his pots and pans.

Then come instructions for gathered worship: do not smother the Spirit, do not look down on prophecy, test everything, keep hold of what is good. Then a solemn charge: “have this letter read to all the brothers and sisters.” This is the first time we hear of a Christian letter being read aloud to a church as a matter of course.

How to read 1 Thessalonians

It takes about fifteen minutes to read aloud, and it is worth reading that way, in a single sitting, as its first hearers did. Then read it again with Acts 17:1–10 open beside it.

Notice how often Paul says “you know”: he is reminding, not informing. Notice the coming of the Lord at the end of every chapter, and how practical the hope is: it makes people holy, hardworking, patient and grateful. If you are grieving, go straight to 4:13–18, and read it as Paul meant it, as words to comfort one another with.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in 1 Thessalonians are worth knowing about before you begin.

“Brothers and sisters.” Paul uses the word adelphoi, literally “brothers”, nearly twenty times in this short letter, more often for its length than anywhere else in his writing. The word took in the whole family of believers, women as well as men, and this edition says “brothers and sisters”. The Open Word Bible lets a reader choose the traditional “brothers” instead.

“Gentle” or “infants” (2:7). Many early manuscripts read “we were infants among you” instead of “we were gentle among you”; the two Greek words differ by a single letter. This translation reads “gentle”, which fits the picture of the nursing mother that follows.

“Your own body” (4:4). The Greek speaks of a “vessel”. It may mean one’s own body, as here, or one’s wife, as in “learn to take a wife for yourself”. The translation follows the first reading.

“Swept up” (4:17). The verb means to seize or snatch suddenly. This translation keeps the suddenness with “swept up”, rather than the more familiar “caught up”.

“The Jews of Judea” (2:14). Paul means those in Judea who persecuted the churches there, and the translation makes that plain, rather than letting the words sound like a statement about the Jewish people as a whole.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: 1 Thessalonians 1
fields.body_html:
Greeting

From Paul, Silvanus and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians, which belongs to God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace and peace to you.

Thanks for the Thessalonians’ faith

Every time we mention you in our prayers, we give thanks to God for all of you. Before our God and Father we never stop remembering the work your faith does, the labor your love takes on, and the endurance your hope in our Lord Jesus Christ gives you. Brothers and sisters loved by God, we know that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in words but also with power, with the Holy Spirit and with full certainty. You know what kind of people we were among you for your sake. You became imitators of us and of the Lord. Though the word brought you great affliction, you received it with joy that came from the Holy Spirit, so that you set an example for every believer in Macedonia and Achaia. The word of the Lord has echoed out from you, and not only through Macedonia and Achaia: in every place people have heard of your faith in God. So there is nothing we need to say. Everywhere people tell of the welcome you gave us, and how you turned to God from idols, to be servants of the living and true God and to wait for his Son from heaven. God raised him from the dead: Jesus, who rescues us from the wrath that is coming.

fields.title: 1 Thessalonians 2
fields.body_html:
Paul’s work among them

You know yourselves, brothers and sisters, that our visit to you was not wasted. We had already suffered and been shamefully treated in Philippi, as you know, but our God gave us courage to tell you his gospel in spite of strong opposition. Our preaching does not come from error or from impure motives, and it uses no deceit. Instead, God has tested us and approved us to be entrusted with the gospel, and that is how we speak: not to please people, but to please God, who tests our hearts. As you know, we never used flattery, and we never put on a show to cover up greed; God is our witness. We did not look for praise from people, whether from you or from anyone else, even though as apostles of Christ we could have made our weight felt. Instead we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother who holds her own children close. Our longing for you was such that we gladly gave you not only the gospel of God but ourselves too, for you had become dear to us.

You remember, brothers and sisters, how hard we worked and toiled: we labored night and day so as not to be a burden to any of you while we preached the gospel of God to you. God is our witness, and so are you: we lived among you believers in a way that was devout, just and without fault. You know how we treated each one of you as a father treats his own children. We urged you on, we comforted you, and we pleaded with you to live in a way that is worthy of God, who is calling you into his own kingdom and glory.

They received God’s own word

And we too give thanks to God without ceasing for this: when you received from us the word of God that you heard, you welcomed it not as a human message but as what it really is, God’s own word, which is now at work in you who believe. For you, brothers and sisters, followed the example of God’s churches in Judea that are in Christ Jesus. You suffered from your own people the same things they suffered from the Jews of Judea, who killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets and drove us out. They do not please God and they are hostile to everyone, because they try to stop us from speaking to the Gentiles so that they may be saved. In this way they keep filling up the full measure of their sins. But the wrath has come upon them at last.

Paul longs to see them

But we, brothers and sisters, were torn away from you for a short time, in person though not in heart, and we longed all the more eagerly to see you face to face. We did want to come to you, and I, Paul, tried more than once, but Satan stood in our way. When our Lord Jesus comes, what will be our hope and joy, the crown we will be proud of before him? Surely it will be you, too. Yes, you are our glory and our joy.

fields.title: 1 Thessalonians 3
fields.body_html:
Timothy sent to strengthen them

So, when we could not bear the waiting any longer, we decided to stay behind in Athens on our own and sent you Timothy, our brother and God’s fellow worker in the gospel of Christ. We sent him to make you strong and to encourage you in your faith, so that none of you would be shaken by these troubles. You know yourselves that we are appointed for this. Even while we were with you, we told you again and again that we were bound to suffer, and it has come about, as you know. So I too, unable to wait any longer, sent Timothy to learn how your faith was standing. I feared the tempter might somehow have tempted you, and our hard work would have come to nothing.

Timothy’s good news

But Timothy has just come back to us from you, with the good news of your faith and love. He tells us that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you. So, brothers and sisters, in all our distress and trouble your faith has given us comfort about you. Now we can truly live again, if you are standing firm in the Lord. What thanks can we give back to God for you, for all the joy we feel before our God because of you? Night and day we pray with great urgency to see you face to face and to fill in whatever is still missing from your faith. Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, clear the way for us to come to you. As for you, may the Lord fill you to overflowing with love for each other and for all people, the kind of love we have for you. Then your hearts will stand firm, without fault and holy before our God and Father when our Lord Jesus comes with all his holy ones.

fields.title: 1 Thessalonians 4
fields.body_html:
A life that pleases God

Finally, brothers and sisters, we ask you and urge you in the Lord Jesus: you learned from us how you ought to live to please God, and you are living that way. Now do so more and more. You know what instructions we gave you by the authority of the Lord Jesus. This is God’s will for you: that you be holy. Keep away from sexual immorality. Each of you should know how to keep your own body under control, with holiness and respect, not in lustful passion like the Gentiles, who do not know God. In this matter no one must cross the line and wrong a brother or sister, for the Lord avenges all such things, as we told you before and solemnly warned you. For God did not call us to be impure, but to live in holiness. So anyone who disregards this is setting aside not a human command but God himself, the God who gives you his Holy Spirit.

Love and quiet work

About love for one another as brothers and sisters, you do not need us to write to you, because God himself has taught you to love each other. And in fact you do love all the brothers and sisters throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers and sisters, to love more and more. Be eager to live calmly, look after your own affairs and earn your living with your hands, as we instructed you, so that outsiders will see you live rightly, and you will not need to rely on anyone.

Those who have fallen asleep

We do not want you to be left in the dark, brothers and sisters, about those who have fallen asleep, so that you do not grieve as others do who have no hope. We believe that Jesus died and rose again; and in the same way, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep. On the Lord’s own authority we tell you this: those of us still living, who remain until the Lord comes, will in no way get there before those who have fallen asleep. The Lord himself will come down from heaven at a shout of command, at an archangel’s call and the sound of God’s trumpet, and the dead who belong to Christ will rise first. Then those of us still living, who are left, will be swept up with them into the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. From then on we will be with the Lord always. So comfort one another with these words.

fields.title: 1 Thessalonians 5
fields.body_html:
The Lord’s day comes like a thief

As for times and dates, brothers and sisters, there is no need for us to write to you. You know very well yourselves that the Lord’s day comes like a thief at night. Just when people are saying, “All is peaceful and safe,” ruin will fall on them without warning, as labor pains come on a woman who is expecting a child, and there will be no escape. But you, brothers and sisters, are not living in darkness, for that day to catch you by surprise like a thief. You are all children of light and children of the day. We do not belong to the night or to darkness. So then, we must not sleep like the rest, but stay awake and keep a clear head. Sleepers sleep at night, and drinkers get drunk at night. But we belong to the day, so let us keep our heads clear, with faith and love for our breastplate and the hope of salvation for our helmet. For God did not destine us for wrath. He destined us to gain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that, awake or asleep, we may live with him together. So keep on encouraging one another and strengthening each other, as you are already doing.

Final instructions

We ask you, brothers and sisters, to recognize those who work hard among you, who lead you in the Lord and correct you. Think of them with the highest respect and love because of the work they do. Keep peace among yourselves. We urge you, brothers and sisters: correct those who are out of line, encourage the fainthearted, stand by the weak, and be patient with everyone. See that no one pays back harm with harm. Always go after what is good, for one another and for all people. Be joyful at all times. Never stop praying. Whatever happens, give thanks; this is what God wants for you in Christ Jesus. Do not smother the Spirit; do not look down on prophecy. Test everything; keep hold of what is good; stay away from evil in every form.

Blessing and farewell

May the God of peace himself make you holy in every part, and may your spirit, soul and body be kept whole and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. The God who calls you can be trusted, and he will do it.

Brothers and sisters, pray for us. Greet all the brothers and sisters with a holy kiss. By the Lord, I solemnly charge you: have this letter read to all the brothers and sisters. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
The Lord himself will come down from heaven at a shout of command, at an archangel’s call and the sound of God’s trumpet, and the dead who belong to Christ will rise first. Then those of us still living, who are left, will be swept up with them into the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. From then on we will be with the Lord always. So comfort one another with these words.

— 1 Thessalonians 4:16–18

The most famous passage in the letter ends with an instruction, not a timetable. Paul has just described the most astonishing event he can imagine, and what he wants the Thessalonians to do with it is to sit with one another in their grief and say these words aloud. The hope of the Lord’s coming, in this letter, is never a puzzle to be solved. It is comfort for the bereaved, courage for the persecuted, and a reason to go on living well.

The question the letter leaves

Paul’s worry in chapter 3 is a simple one: are they standing firm? It is the question the letter leaves with every reader. The Thessalonians had heard the gospel for a few weeks, from men who were then driven out of town. They had lost friends and family to persecution and death. They might easily have drifted back to the gods of the city. Instead, Timothy found them still believing, still loving, still waiting.

What kept them was not their own strength. Paul is clear that the word they received was “God’s own word, which is now at work in you who believe”, and that the God who called them “can be trusted, and he will do it.” But they had to keep hold of it, and they had to keep hold of each other. That is why the letter ends with so many commands about life together: encourage, correct, stand by, be patient, pray. A faith that stands firm is rarely a solitary one.

Where the letter points

It points forward, to the day when the living and the dead in Christ will be together with the Lord. It points inward, to holiness of body and heart, to a quiet and honest life, to joy and prayer and thanks in every circumstance. And it points onward, to a second letter. Some in Thessalonica came to think the day of the Lord had already arrived, and a second letter was sent to steady them. The Second Letter to the Thessalonians, in this same edition, is the natural next thing to read.

Where to go from here

Many of the church’s great teachers have written on the themes of this letter, and several of them are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On holiness (4:3 and 5:23). J. C. Ryle’s Holiness, whose chapter on sanctification takes 4:3 as its text; John Wesley’s A Plain Account of Christian Perfection, which leans on Paul’s prayer that God would make them holy in every part; and A. B. Simpson’s sermon Wholly Sanctified, on 5:23–24.
  • On the hope of the Lord’s coming (4:13–18). Richard Baxter’s The Saints’ Everlasting Rest, written when he thought himself dying, which draws on this passage in describing the resurrection and the life with the Lord that follows it.
  • On prayer without ceasing (5:17). Brother Lawrence’s The Practice of the Presence of God, from a monastery kitchen in Paris, and E. M. Bounds’s The Necessity of Prayer.
  • On praying for one another (5:25). George Whitefield’s sermon Intercession Every Christian’s Duty, on Paul’s request, “Brothers and sisters, pray for us.”
  • On the Spirit in the church (5:19). A. B. Simpson’s Hindering the Holy Spirit, which takes up “do not smother the Spirit” beside two other texts.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to 1 Thessalonians in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this letter.

But the best next step may be to read the letter again, aloud, as Paul charged that it be read. It is short enough for one sitting and warm enough to be heard as what it is: a father’s letter to children he could not stop thinking about. And his prayer for them may become a prayer for you:

May the God of peace himself make you holy in every part, and may your spirit, soul and body be kept whole and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. The God who calls you can be trusted, and he will do it.

— 1 Thessalonians 5:23–24
